t: Introduction: the topic and its significance
n: This lesson is devoted to poisoning with drugs and narcotics. According to the United Nations, in the world 130–190 million people use cannabis preparations, 30–40 million use amphetamine-type preparations, and 11.3 million use heroin. Cannabis and opiates have a sedative, that is, calming, effect, whereas cocaine and amphetamines are stimulant. Poisoning with sleeping drugs results from suicide or accident. The aim of the lesson: to study the signs and examination of poisoning with cannabis and other narcotics, and with medicinal substances such as sleeping drugs, atropine and clonidine.

t: Poisoning with sleeping drugs (barbiturates)
n: Sleeping drugs include derivatives of barbituric acid: luminal, veronal, Nembutal, and also noxiron and tetridin. Tranquillisers, that is, Elenium, Seduxen and meprobamate, also induce sleep. These substances depress the central nervous system. Clinically, deep sleep, fall of pressure and temperature, disturbed breathing and coma are seen. Death results from paralysis of the respiratory centre. Lethal doses: for barbamyl and Nembutal 1.0–2.0 g, for medinal and tetridin 3.0–5.0 g, for noxiron 5.0–10 g. In the elderly a smaller amount may be fatal. Remember: alcohol or other sedatives intensify the effect.

t: Sleeping drugs: the body and forensic diagnosis
n: Barbiturates, besides depressing the central nervous system, also increase the permeability of blood vessels. Today, short-acting barbiturates, for example cyclobarbital, are mainly used as sleeping drugs; the others are more often used as anticonvulsants. In the body mainly signs of rapid death are found, and there are no changes characteristic of sleeping drugs. Tablet residues may be present in the stomach. Diagnosis rests on the circumstances of the event, the clinical picture and the forensic chemical result. Because a therapeutic dose is possible, quantitative examination is necessary. In a treatment institution, besides blood and urine, gastric lavage fluid is also taken.

t: CNS stimulant poisons: strychnine, psychotonics
n: Now poisons that stimulate the central nervous system. Psychotonics, that is, caffeine, phenamine and phenatine, raise the tone of the higher parts. In a large dose acute psychosis occurs with tremor, convulsions, tachycardia, raised pressure and delirium. Antidepressants, that is, imizin, indopan and curedal, are monoamine oxidase inhibitors. In a toxic dose headache, vomiting, raised temperature and pressure, and rhythm disturbance are seen. With regular intake, dependence develops. Strychnine, however, is an alkaloid of nux vomica seeds, and increases the excitability of the spinal cord.

t: Strychnine: clinical picture and forensic significance
n: Strychnine is an alkaloid of the seeds of nux vomica and "emetic root". It increases the reflex excitability of the spinal cord and is excreted slowly through the kidneys. Clinically, movement, breathing and swallowing first become difficult, the muscles draw up, then attacks of tonic convulsions begin; consciousness is retained. The face turns blue, the pupils dilate, and the body arches, which is called opisthotonus. Light, sound or touch provokes a new attack. The lethal dose is 0.1–0.3 g for adults and 0.005 g for small children. In the body rigor develops quickly and strongly. Strychnine is a stable poison and persists in the body for months.

t: Poisons acting on the CNS and PNS
n: Substances of this group act on the transmission of the impulse at nerve endings, that is, on mediators. Muscle relaxants block the impulse at the neuromuscular synapse; death results from paralysis of the respiratory muscles, and there are no specific signs. We compare the main substances. With atropine the pupil is dilated and delirium is seen; lethal dose 0.1 g of atropine sulphate. With pilocarpine the pupil is constricted and much sweat and saliva are secreted; lethal dose 0.06 g. With pachycarpine there are convulsions, disturbed vision and collapse; lethal dose 1.0–2.0 g. With clonidine pressure falls, and bradycardia and sleep are seen; for adults 0.005–0.01 g. Attention: atropine dilates the pupil and pilocarpine constricts it; do not confuse them.

t: Atropine poisoning
n: Atropine is an alkaloid contained in belladonna, henbane and thorn apple. Poisoning is seen when too large a dose is accidentally given, or on eating the plant. Within 10–15 minutes the face reddens, the mouth and throat dry, the pupil dilates and vision is disturbed; then delirium and hallucinations begin. Swallowing becomes difficult, the voice is hoarse, the pulse quickens, and atony of the intestine and bladder develops. The lethal dose of atropine sulphate for adults is 0.1 g. Death results from cardiac arrest or paralysis of the respiratory centre. Atropine is stable: it persists in the body for several months, so the forensic chemical result is the main evidence.

t: Poisoning with pilocarpine and pachycarpine
n: Pilocarpine poisoning usually occurs when the preparation is given by mistake in a large dose. Dizziness, flushing, profuse sweating and salivation, constriction of the pupil, tachycardia, dyspnoea, abdominal pain and diarrhoea are seen; bronchospasm and pulmonary oedema also develop. The lethal dose of pilocarpine is 0.06 g. In the body, constriction of the pupil and much mucus in the airways are found. Pachycarpine is an n-cholinolytic and acts strongly on the muscles of the uterus; poisoning is possible in an attempt to terminate pregnancy. The lethal dose of pachycarpine is 1.0–2.0 g. There are no specific signs in the body, so forensic chemical examination is decisive.

t: Case analysis and quick question: drug poisonings
n: We consider the case analysis. Clonidine, that is, an alpha-adrenergic blocker, has been added to a drink. Recently such cases of deliberate poisoning have become more frequent. Signs: dizziness, marked weakness, drowsiness, persistent fall of blood pressure, bradycardia and loss of consciousness. The lethal dose for adults is 0.005–0.01 g. Attention, there is a risk of error: atropine is not pilocarpine. With atropine the pupil dilates, with pilocarpine it constricts. Quick question: the pupil is wide, the mouth and throat are dry, the face is red, and there is delirium. Which substance? Remember, with pilocarpine much sweat and saliva are secreted.

t: Clonidine and muscle relaxants: the expert's view
n: Clonidine is an alpha-adrenergic blocker; recently cases of deliberate poisoning by adding it to a drink have become more frequent. Signs: dizziness, marked weakness, drowsiness, persistent fall of blood pressure, bradycardia, hypothermia and loss of consciousness. The lethal dose of clonidine is 0.005–0.01 g for adults and 0.004 g or less for children. Muscle relaxants, that is, listenon, tubarine and ditilin, block the neuromuscular synapse; death results from paralysis of the respiratory muscles. There are no specific changes in the body. Venous congestion, pulmonary oedema and haemorrhages under the serous and mucous membranes are possible.

t: Narcotic and psychotropic substances: general concepts
n: General concepts of narcotic and psychotropic substances. United Nations data: cannabis is used by 130–190 million, heroin by 11.3 million people. DRD is death connected with these narcotics: poisoning, suicide, accident, homicide. Precursors are substances used in making narcotics, and include potassium permanganate, acetone and ephedrine. By origin narcotics fall into three groups. Natural: cannabis, morphine, codeine, cocaine. Semisynthetic: heroin, mescaline, ephedrone. Synthetic: amphetamine, promedol, methadone, sombrevin.

t: Opiates, cocaine and amphetamines
n: Opiates are quickly absorbed into the blood and accumulate more in the liver. About 90 % of morphine is excreted in the first 3–4 days. Attention: with opiates the euphoria is calming, whereas with cocaine it is accompanied by excitation; death from cocaine may also be from fibrillation. Amphetamines are similar to cocaine but weaker and longer-acting; repeated intake causes dependence. Lethal doses are in the table. When dried opium is taken by mouth, coma and paralysis of the respiratory centre occur; dose 2–5 g. Morphine by mouth: pupil constricted, coma, 0.2–0.4 g. Morphine parenterally: the same effect, 0.1–0.2 g. Ecstasy, that is, MDMA, stimulates the central nervous system; dose 500 mg.

t: Opiates: absorption, elimination and lethal doses
n: The juice of the opium poppy contains morphine, codeine, thebaine and narcotine. Heroin, by contrast, is a semisynthetic product of opium, that is, acetylated morphine. Taken by mouth, the action begins in 20–30 minutes, and by subcutaneous injection in 10–15 minutes. In the liver the concentration of morphine is about five times that in the blood. Peak elimination of morphine is at 8–12 hours; in the first 3–4 days about 90 per cent is excreted. Signs: nausea, vomiting, cyanosis, constriction of the pupil, dyspnoea and coma; death from paralysis of the respiratory centre. Lethal dose: dried opium by mouth 2–5 g, morphine 0.2–0.4 g, parenterally 0.1–0.2 g. Morphine persists in the body for months.

t: Poisoning with cannabis preparations
n: The main narcotic component of cannabis is tetrahydrocannabinol. It is smoked or taken by mouth; the pupil dilates, nystagmus and tachycardia are seen, and blood pressure rises. Cannabis breaks down quickly, so poisoning usually does not end in death. If the package carried in the gastrointestinal tract by a drug courier is breached, death is possible. Spices are smoking mixtures in which a synthetic cannabinoid has been added to a plant. They act more strongly and for longer than cannabis; tremor, convulsions and hallucinations occur. For a cannabinoid, 10 ml of blood, 10 ml of urine, 10 ml of saliva and a rinse from the fingers of the hand are taken. The fingers are wiped with alcohol-soaked cotton, dried and placed in a bag.

t: Cocaine, psychotropic substances and amphetamines
n: Cocaine is obtained from coca leaves. The powder is snorted through the nose, and the solution is injected into a vein or under the skin. With cocaine, euphoria with psychomotor excitation and dilatation of the pupil are seen; death results from paralysis of the respiratory centre or ventricular fibrillation. LSD, psilocybin, phencyclidine and mescaline cause autonomic disturbance and mental disturbance, that is, hallucinations. Amphetamines are synthetic derivatives of phenylethylamine; they are similar to cocaine but weaker and longer-acting, and intravenous injection is dangerous. "Ecstasy", that is, MDMA, is distributed as club tablets; its lethal dose is 500 mg.

t: Dependence, tolerance and precursors
n: Repeated intake leads to psychological dependence and tolerance; tolerance is physical dependence. When intake is stopped, a withdrawal syndrome occurs. Habituation to opiates develops on average in 25–30 days, and the dose may rise to 10.0 g a day; withdrawal lasts 5–6 days. Precursors are substances used in making narcotics: hydrochloric and sulphuric acids, potassium permanganate, ethyl ether, acetone, toluene, ephedrine and others. Separate requirements are laid down for the purchase, storage and writing off of precursors.

t: Material for the laboratory and times of detection in urine
n: Rules for taking material for the laboratory. For cannabinoids, 10 ml of blood, 10 ml of urine, 10 ml of saliva and a rinse from the fingers of the hand are taken. For other narcotics, 15–20 ml of blood and at least 200 ml of urine are taken from the suspect. Times of detection in urine, that is, after what time and for how long it is detected: cannabinoids 1–3 hours and 24–168 hours; heroin 2–6 hours and 24–72 hours. Methamphetamine 4–6 hours and 48–72 hours; cocaine 2–6 hours and 48–72 hours; phencyclidine 4–6 hours and 7–14 days.

t: Narcotics: detection in urine and signs on the body
n: Changes in the body fall into four groups; specific neurochemical changes have no importance in practice. Along the veins, small ulcer-scars and infections introduced by injection, for example hepatitis, are found. These signs are indirect evidence: they are assessed together with the circumstances of the event and the forensic chemical results. The table shows detection in urine. Cannabinoids begin at 1–3 hours and last 24–168 hours. Heroin begins at 2–6 hours and lasts 24–72 hours. Cocaine 2–6 hours and 48–72 hours. Phencyclidine 4–6 hours and 7–14 days.

t: Changes in the body of a narcotic user
n: Specific neurochemical changes are detected only in experiment or within a very short time after death; they have no importance in practice. With intravenous use, small ulcers and scars of different ages are found along the veins; from non-sterile solutions vasculitis, thrombophlebitis, bacterial endocarditis and sepsis develop. With intake through the nose there are chronic inflammation of the nasal mucosa, aspiration pneumonia and granulomas in the lungs. Diseases transmitted by injection: AIDS, hepatitis D, C and B. Traces of lifestyle: emaciation, tuberculosis, tattoos. These signs are indirect evidence; they are assessed together with the circumstances of the event, the clinical picture and, mainly, the forensic chemical results.

t: Conclusion and main findings
n: We conclude. In poisoning with sleeping drugs, strychnine, atropine, clonidine and muscle relaxants, specific signs in the body are absent or few; the forensic chemical result is decisive. Opiates and cannabis have a sedative effect, and cocaine and amphetamines a stimulant one; morphine persists in the body for months. The material, that is, blood, urine, saliva and rinse, must be taken as quickly and correctly as possible. Signs in the body pointing to narcotic use are indirect evidence and are assessed together with forensic chemical examination.
